headline: The competition between strike systems and air defense/interceptor systems continues to evolve on both sides. In response to Russia’s growing use of jet-powered Geran-4 loitering munitions and Geran-5/Banderol cruise missiles, Ukraine has begun developing jet-powered interceptor drones. The aim is to address a class of faster aerial threats that can be difficult for conventional propeller-driven interceptors to engage. Ukraine has also used Bars jet-powered drones in at least one strike campaign against Moscow. Their numbers are still believed to be limited, with propeller-driven drones making up the majority of Ukraine’s long-range strike fleet. This highlights a broader issue for Russia: the need to develop and deploy compact interceptor drones before faster targets become more widespread. The challenge is not simply intercepting them, but doing so economically. Traditional air-defense systems and MANPADS can engage such targets, but using them against relatively inexpensive strike drones can be difficult to justify economically. One potentially relevant example comes from Iran. Several years ago, Iran developed and deployed the 358 missile, a specialized system intended to engage UAVs. It is a subsonic weapon with a reported speed of around 700 km/h, an infrared seeker, and a turbojet engine, with a claimed engagement range of up to 100 km. Its design reflects a different approach to countering relatively slow aerial targets, without relying on the speed and cost associated with conventional high-performance surface-to-air missiles. The missile has demonstrated its effectiveness, having shot down a number of U.S. and Israeli UAVs. This is not necessarily an argument for simply copying the 358. The more important point is anticipating what types of drones may be heading toward Russian cities in the future and developing an interceptor that is capable of engaging them while remaining cheaper than the strike systems it is designed to counter.

headline: Boeing has delivered the 22nd F-15EX Eagle II to the U.S. Air Force, and the aircraft is the first F-15EX destined for permanent assignment to the 67th Fighter Squadron at Kadena Air Base, Japan. The aircraft departed Boeing's St. Louis facility on August 28 and is currently at Portland Air National Guard Base, Oregon, where it will receive additional preparation before eventually moving to Kadena. The first permanently stationed F-15EXs are expected to begin arriving at Kadena during fiscal year 2027, which begins October 1st. The Air Force has said the F-15EX will bring advanced avionics, enhanced survivability, modern electronic-warfare systems and increased weapons capacity to Kadena, while the transition period is intended to give Airmen experience operating and sustaining the aircraft before it becomes a permanent part of the wing. Kadena is ultimately planned to receive 36 F-15EXs to replace its aging F-15C/D fleet.

headline: Newsweek reports that the USS Abraham Lincoln will make another port stop before returning to the United States, extending a deployment that has already lasted 286 days. The carrier was originally expected home in early summer but was diverted from the IndoPacific to the Middle East in January to support U.S. operations during the Iran war. A family member of a Lincoln sailor told Newsweek that the additional stop is needed because the carrier still has to fulfill time originally assigned to the IndoPacific after being diverted. The Navy has not independently confirmed that explanation, and Newsweek notes that multiple port visits during a carrier's return phase are not unusual and can serve maintenance, logistical, diplomatic and crew welfare purposes. Publicly available Navy material also does not establish that carriers must “make up” a fixed number of days after a diversion. The Lincoln arrived in Thailand on Sept. 2 after approximately 250 days without a port visit, allowing roughly 5,000 sailors and Marines to go ashore. The Navy says the carrier will return as part of a planned rotation, while congressional lawmakers have raised questions about the deployment's effect on service member well being, maintenance schedules and fleet readiness. Source: https://www.newsweek.com/uss-abraham-lincoln-thailand-port-stop-heading-home-explainer-12402308 Photo: https://www.thainewspix.com/en/preview/55512

headline: Secretary of Interior Doug Burgum announced that excavation work is set to begin for the Great Triumphal Arch and Military Observation Deck at Memorial Circle on Columbia Island, between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. Burgum says the project fulfills a vision that dates back more than 125 years. The 1902 McMillan Commission called for a monumental treatment at the western terminus of Arlington Memorial Bridge, while the 1924 Arlington Memorial Bridge Commission described Columbia Island as an appropriate site for a formal park and plaza connecting the bridge with Arlington Cemetery. According to Burgum, the site instead became a largely undeveloped traffic circle. The planned arch is intended to provide the monumental treatment envisioned in those earlier plans, with Burgum describing it as a major work of American architecture honoring the history and significance of Arlington National Cemetery. He also noted that Washington, D.C., is unusual among major Western capitals in lacking a major triumphal arch.

headline: Military Times reports that a federal appeals court has restored Bowe Bergdahl’s 2017 court martial conviction, overturning a 2023 decision that vacated it. A three judge D.C. Circuit panel ruled that the civilian district court did not have jurisdiction to overturn the military judgment, saying collateral review of court martial convictions must remain within the military justice system. Bergdahl pleaded guilty in 2017 to desertion and misbehavior before the enemy after walking away from his Afghanistan post in 2009 and being captured by the Taliban. The search for him resulted in severe injuries to other U.S. troops and the death of a military working dog. He was dishonorably discharged and ordered to forfeit $10,000 in pay, but received no prison sentence after presenting evidence of torture and abuse in captivity. The 2023 ruling had vacated the conviction after finding that the military judge had failed to disclose an application for an executive-branch immigration judge position, potentially creating a conflict of interest. Bergdahl’s attorneys also argued that Donald Trump’s public calls for Bergdahl to be severely punished, including a call for execution during the 2016 campaign, created improper command influence. The appeals court did not rule on either of those underlying issues. Bergdahl’s attorney says the case still raises serious questions about the integrity of the military justice system, and his legal team has 45 days to consider seeking reconsideration or Supreme Court review. Source: https://www.militarytimes.com/news/your-military/2026/09/03/court-overturns-2023-ruling-that-wiped-bowe-bergdahls-conviction/

headline: CBS News reports that the Pentagon officially ended Operation Epic Fury on May 5, but an Air Force email dated Aug. 7 instructed military leaders to stop using the operation’s name when referring to ongoing U.S. military activity against Iran. Instead, personnel were told to use broader language such as “overseas operations in the CENTCOM Area of Responsibility.” The guidance reportedly went beyond the Air Force and was disseminated across the Defense Department. The Pentagon says subsequent activities included Freedom of Navigation operations and strikes against IRGC threats to commercial shipping, Gulf countries and U.S. forces. Trump formally notified Congress on July 7 that U.S. military action against Iran had restarted after the April ceasefire collapsed. The timing has also created questions about casualty accounting. Four service members killed in July were initially categorized by the Defense Department as killed during Operation Epic Fury, despite the Pentagon now saying the operation ended May 5. They were subsequently moved into a new “overseas operations” category, reducing the recorded Epic Fury deaths from 18 to 14. The Pentagon attributed the earlier classification to a “temporary data disruption,” while the current casualty system still contains apparent inconsistencies, including June wounded and a July death listed under Epic Fury. The broader issue is that the Pentagon now acknowledges a May 5 end date that it previously declined to provide publicly, even though U.S. and Iranian forces continued exchanging fire and U.S. military operations related to the conflict continued afterward. Source: https://www.cbsnews.com/news/military-operation-epic-fury-may-5/
